title: Krishna Destroys the Flying City Saubha and Slays Shalva
story:
For one more hour the flying city Saubha hung over the sea like a slow storm — the last storm the coast of Dwaraka would ever fear.

It had been a war unlike any Dwaraka had known: no army to meet, no gate to storm, only an enemy that drifted with the wind and rained destruction from above. Saubha was no fortress; it was a kingdom with wings, a floating capital no army had ever taken, and Shalva had ruled it for years beyond the reach of every enemy he had made. Krishna had answered him from the ground for days, and now the duel had narrowed to its end. Shalva's sorcery had failed him; his weapons had been shattered one by one; the king who had fought from an unreachable sky was running out of sky.

He came down one final time, rushing at Krishna with everything left to him, and Krishna met him with arrows that struck true through pride and armor alike. They pierced his guard, cut through his war-plate, snapped his bow, and tore the jewel from his crest. Nor had Krishna's own chariot come through the war untouched: his horses stood thick with shafts, and Daruka his charioteer, pierced and faint, confessed that he could barely hold the reins. Krishna cheered him. Hold on, he said — the driver's place was at the reins, and he himself would not fail him; the battle would not last forever.

And in that moment of weakness Krishna did what he had come to do. He took up his mace and turned it on the city itself: the blow that might have been spent on a king was spent on a kingdom. The mace struck Saubha's hull, and the flying city — the wonder of its age, the terror of the coast, the thing no army could reach — came apart and fell into the sea in a thousand fragments, and the water swallowed them like rain. Men would say afterward that it had gone down as the three cities of the demons went down in the oldest tales, blasted from the sky.

Where a city had floated there was now only sky — and Shalva. City gone, weapons gone, he came at Krishna on foot, mace in hand, with nothing left but fury. Fury was not enough. As he rushed in, Krishna severed the arm that held the mace; the weapon fell beside its owner, and the king of Saubha stood weaponless at last.

Then Krishna raised the discus, which blazed like the sun at the world's end, and for a moment it hung in the air like a second sun while every eye on the field followed it. Then it fell, and in one clean sweep it cut off Shalva's crowned head; where it passed, the enemy burned. The king who had lived above the world was gathered into it at last.

The war was over. The sea smoothed itself over the scattered stones of Saubha, the sky above Dwaraka was only sky again, and the grudge that had darkened it was ended. Shalva, who had raided the coast, who had conjured a dead father before his son's eyes, who had fought from a city no army could reach, lay in the dust at last, where his enmity could trouble no one anymore.
reflection: The fall of Saubha is total: city, weapons, and king gone in a single hour, and the Bhagavata gives each its own instrument — the mace for the kingdom, the discus for the king. The image of the discus blazing like the sun at the world's end turns the end of a tyrant into a kind of sunrise: destruction, but destruction that clears the sky.
tradition_note: In the Mahabharata, the discus alone finishes the war: it cuts Saubha in two like a saw through a tall tree, then cleaves Shalva as he raises his mace. The Bhagavata Purana gives the mace the task of shattering the city and the discus the beheading; this story follows the Bhagavata.
content_note: Mild violence: Shalva's arm is severed and he is beheaded; described without gore.
next_story_tease: The news of Shalva's end would not travel far before another enemy rose to answer for it.
hero_scene: Krishna, standing in his chariot, hurls the blazing discus against the onrushing Shalva as the shattered fragments of the flying city Saubha fall like rain into the sea behind them.
